structure.title: Act I, scenes 1–3 · The duke lends his office to another man
structure.text: Vienna's neglected sexual laws acquire an energetic enforcer in Angelo. Claudio is sentenced for getting his intended wife pregnant. The duke has ostensibly left town, but a friar begins taking a remarkable interest in the city's affairs.

structure.title: Act I, scene 4 – Act II · Isabella petitions the deputy
structure.text: About to join a convent, Claudio's sister takes his case to Angelo. He hears her unusually well, with consequences she could scarcely have anticipated. A public official can determine what happens in a private room and whose report of it will be believed.

structure.title: Acts III–V · Substitutions and a public hearing
structure.text: The disguised duke arranges encounters and relays instructions through a prison. Later, a public hearing appears to offer an injured person an ordinary route to justice. The audience knows how much of the testimony the judge has already helped to produce.

people.name: Isabella
people.text: She can argue powerfully for mercy while holding herself to a severe standard. Her brother's dependence on her makes it nearly impossible to have a disinterested conversation about whose body may pay for whose life.

people.name: Angelo and the duke
people.text: Angelo's reputation for discipline is part of his qualification for office. The duke can hear people talk about his government because they believe him elsewhere. Each exercises forms of power hidden from the petitioners in front of him.

context.title: An old law suddenly enforced
context.text: A practice tolerated for years can become a capital offence the moment a new official decides to apply the law. Claudio's neighbours understand his conduct differently from the deputy who makes him the first example.

notice.text: Whose proposal must Isabella answer immediately?
notice.why: Men with claims upon her time arrange deadlines, meetings and decisions. A pause onstage may be the only room she gets to weigh an offer on her own terms.
Someone must keep track of actual people, hours and bodies. A scheme for dispensing perfect justice looks different from the working side of a cell door.

opening: A ruler puts his morally rigorous deputy in charge of a city accustomed to ignoring its own laws. When the deputy sentences a young man to death, the man's sister comes to plead for him. Her appeal awakens a desire the official has no intention of applying his principles to honestly. Shakespeare places a woman with almost no public power before a man whose reputation makes him difficult to accuse, exposing what happens when the authority to punish comes with control over whose story will be believed.
